terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Set a setting for one command with `ORDERS_LIMIT=2 node orders.js list orders/press-1.txt` (PowerShell: `$env:ORDERS_LIMIT=2` first).

tasks.title: Take a setting from the environment, and let a flag win
tasks.description:
Write `withSettings(flags, env)` in `src/settings.js`, and use it in `orders.js`.

- it returns the flags it was given, with `limit` taken from `env.ORDERS_LIMIT` when no `--limit` was typed, as text, like a typed value
- a typed `--limit` or `-n` always wins, and then `ORDERS_LIMIT` is not looked at at all
- with no `ORDERS_LIMIT` and no flag, nothing is added
- an `ORDERS_LIMIT` that is not a whole number above 0 makes it throw an `Error` whose message names `ORDERS_LIMIT`, so the person knows which setting to fix
- `orders.js` runs each command with `withSettings(flags, process.env)`, so `ORDERS_LIMIT=3 node orders.js list` lists three orders

The check calls `withSettings` with flags and environments of its own, and runs `node orders.js list` with `ORDERS_LIMIT` set, with `-n` typed too, and with a broken setting.
nextSteps: Read "Settings from the environment" in the lesson.
Write `withSettings`: decide first whether the setting is used at all.
Check the setting before you use it, and name it when it is wrong.
In `orders.js`, pass the flags through it before running the command, and try `ORDERS_LIMIT=2 node orders.js list orders/press-1.txt`.
hints: A setting says what this computer usually wants; a flag says what the person wants this once. So the setting only fills a gap the flags left.
`flags.limit === undefined` says no limit was typed. Giving back a new object with `{ ...flags, limit }` leaves the flags readArgs made as they were. A whole number above 0 matches `/^[1-9]\d*$/`.

`if (flags.limit !== undefined || env.ORDERS_LIMIT === undefined) return flags`, then throw `new Error(`ORDERS_LIMIT must be a whole number above 0, not "${env.ORDERS_LIMIT}"`)` when it does not match, and otherwise `return { ...flags, limit: env.ORDERS_LIMIT }`.

tasks.title: Colour only for a person at a terminal
tasks.description:
Write `useColour(stream, env)` in `src/settings.js`, and colour the problems that `check` finds.

- `useColour` returns `true` only when `stream.isTTY` is `true` and `env.NO_COLOR` is not set; `NO_COLOR` set to the empty text counts as not set
- in `orders.js`, ask it as `useColour(process.stdout, process.env)`; once is enough
- when it says yes, `check` prints each problem line in red: `\x1b[31m` before the text and `\x1b[39m` after it, the words unchanged
- with `--json`, or when it says no, nothing the tool prints holds a colour code

A check cannot give the tool a real terminal, so it stands in for one: it sets `process.stdout.isTTY` to `true` before the tool starts, and `TERM` in its environment, as a terminal does.

The check calls `useColour` with streams and environments of its own, and runs `check` at a stand-in terminal, with `NO_COLOR` set, into a pipe, and with `--json`.
nextSteps: Run `node orders.js check orders/press-2.txt`, then the same with `> out.txt` and look in the file: no colour codes must ever end up there.
Read "Colour, but only for people" in the lesson.
Write `useColour` from the stream it is given and the environment.
In `orders.js`, wrap each problem line of `check` when it says yes.
hints: Colour codes are characters like any other. A person at a terminal sees red; a file or a program sees `\x1b[31m` in the middle of its text.
`process.stdout.isTTY` is `true` only for a terminal; for a file or a pipe it is `undefined`. An empty `NO_COLOR` is falsy, which is what the custom wants.

`return stream.isTTY === true && !env.NO_COLOR`. In `main`, `const red = command === 'check' && useColour(process.stdout, process.env)`, and in `out.result` print `red ? `\x1b[31m${text}\x1b[39m` : text` when `--json` is off.

tasks.title: Give the tool a name, and rewrite the morning
tasks.description:
Make `orders` a tool with a name, and put it to work.

- the very first line of `orders.js` is `#!/usr/bin/env node`
- `package.json` has a `bin` entry that gives the command `orders` and points at `orders.js`: `"bin": { "orders": "orders.js" }`
- `morning.txt` holds three commands of the tool in place of the three old ones, one on each line, in the same order: how many orders there are, how many on each paper, and which lines are broken. Each starts with `orders`, names both files, `orders/press-1.txt orders/press-2.txt`, and uses plain words only: no quotes, pipes or patterns. Lines that start with `#` are comments and may stay

Nothing has to be installed: `node orders.js` does what `orders` will do once the shop installs it.

The check reads the first line of `orders.js` and the `bin` entry, and runs each command of `morning.txt` as `node orders.js ...` with order files of its own at those two paths.
nextSteps: Read "A name of its own" and "The morning" in the lesson.
Add the first line to `orders.js` and the `bin` entry to `package.json`.
Work out which command and flags answer each of the three questions in `morning.txt`.
Try each one as `node orders.js ...` before you write it down.
hints: The `#!` line must be the first two characters of the file. `/usr/bin/env node` finds `node` wherever it is installed, instead of naming one place.
`bin` maps the name a person types to the file that runs. The old commands counted lines, counted by the fourth field, and looked for broken lines; your tool has a command and a flag for each.
`orders count orders/press-1.txt orders/press-2.txt`, `orders count --by paper orders/press-1.txt orders/press-2.txt` and `orders check orders/press-1.txt orders/press-2.txt`.
